title: Carrying tales
hookLine: telling someone what another said about them

cards: In Genesis, Sarah overhears a visitor promise that she will have a son, and she laughs to herself. She's old, she thinks, and her husband is old too.
Then God speaks to Abraham about the laugh, and repeats what Sarah said. Listen closely to the repeat. God reports that Sarah wondered whether she, being old, could bear a child.
The part about Abraham being old is gone. The Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, noticed the missing words, and it says God left them out for the sake of peace in the home.

teach.h: NOT A TALEBEARER AMONG THY PEOPLE.
teach.b: Rechilut. Carrying tales: telling someone what another person said or did about them. Turn it four ways.
First, the verse. Leviticus says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." Up and down, from house to house.
Second, another peddler. Yesterday's peddler sold life.

teach.h: LIKE A PEDDLER, DOOR TO DOOR.
teach.b: Rashi connects the word for talebearer with the trader who walks door to door with a pack.
As Rashi describes it, the talebearer works a similar route: going into people's houses to find something bad, then telling it in the market. Third, what makes it different.
The Chafetz Chaim treats rechilut as its own kind of harmful speech. Lashon hara lowers someone in others' eyes.
Rechilut aims at a relationship. So-and-so said this about you. Your sister thinks you're selfish.
The words may be accurate, and the carrier may even think they're helping. But two people at peace an hour ago now aren't.
Fourth, what God left out, an edit you may remember from early on as peace over precision.
The full report was available, and accurate. In the Talmud's reading, God edits it for peace between a husband and wife. No one is asked to invent anything.
The question is simpler: when you know what someone said about someone else, do they need to hear it? Or does the story only want a carrier?

how: Jews who study the laws of speech learn rechilut as its own category alongside lashon hara, and the tradition of editing a report for the sake of peace is often taught from the Talmud's reading of Sarah's laugh.

o: keeping a secret that should have been told
carrying tales from one person to another
telling lies about someone in a court of law

p: the talebearer is like a peddler
laughed: her husband is old too

s: rechilut only counts if the tale is false
the words may be accurate; what makes it rechilut is carrying them to the person they're about.
the Talmud says God changed Sarah's words for the sake of peace
Yevamot notices that God's report to Abraham leaves out the part about Abraham being old.

lashon hara lowers someone in others' eyes; rechilut aims at a relationship.

games.q: Sarah has laughed, saying she is old and her husband is old too. God tells Abraham about the laugh. what does God report?
o: every word, including that Abraham is old.
only that Sarah wondered whether she, being old, could bear a child.
games.why: the part about Abraham is gone. the Talmud, in Yevamot, says God changed the words for the sake of peace.

practice: Let one remark come to mind that someone made about someone else, which the second person doesn't know yet: a comment at work, in the family, a screenshot.
Picture the two of them still at peace, and ask whether passing it on would protect anyone or only move a hurt from one house to another.
If it protects no one, set it down like a peddler putting down a pack; if you pray, you can ask for peace between them.

wordCard.voice: Rechilut. Carrying tales: going from one person to another with what was said about them, like a peddler with a pack. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: talebearing; Rashi links it to the traveling trader.

carryVoice: Your line: don't carry tales. A story with no carrier stops where it is. Go in peace.

sources.q: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people
